title: Biblical Prophecy Evidence
scope: 22 researched prophecy source-to-later-use cases in three batches. Matthew's ten fulfillment formulas covered; a 50-claim seed inventory now includes five additional NT cases studied. Independent outside review deferred until defined inventory and scope are complete.
method: Do not treat a later narrative quoting an earlier passage as independent proof that the event happened. Record composition/redaction dating separately from the story's setting; a date is 'undetermined' if uncertain. Do not equate resemblance with historical causation. Do not call a retrospective lament or Exodus memory a failed forward prediction; do not automatically label a partial fulfillment as complete. A conditional warning must be assessed as a warning. Distinguish lexical variants from theological interpretations and from historical evidence. No binary overall truth-score.

records.label: The young woman and Immanuel
records.kind: Contemporary sign later reapplied
records.original: הָעַלְמָה (ha-‘almah; the young woman)
records.setting: Isaiah addresses King Ahaz during a military crisis in Judah; the child functions as a sign within a near-term political timetable (see 7:15–16).
records.laterUse: Matthew quotes the Greek-scripture form using parthenos and applies it to Mary's conception of Jesus.
records.relationship: Retrospective messianic rereading, with a Hebrew-to-Greek lexical change.
records.evidence: The connection is explicit in Matthew. The Hebrew noun alone does not require a miraculous conception; the supernatural claim is part of Matthew's narrative and not independently established.
records.sourceStatus: Original-context reading strong; historical miracle unverified
refs: TheTorah: Jewish origins of Christmas story
Yale Bible Study: Matthew ancestry and birth

records.label: Out of Egypt I called my son
records.kind: Past narrative later reapplied
records.original: כִּי נַעַר יִשְׂרָאֵל (when Israel was a boy)
records.setting: Hosea recalls the historical Exodus story and addresses Israel as God's wayward child; its verbs point back to a past relationship.
records.laterUse: Matthew cites Hosea 11:1 immediately after narrating the family's flight into Egypt (Matthew 2:14–15), although their return from Egypt is narrated later (2:19–21).
records.relationship: Matthew identifies Jesus with Israel by typology. Seong-Kwang Kevin Kim (2019) notes that the quotation about coming out is placed before Matthew narrates the return and offers a larger Israel/Egypt pattern to explain the application.
records.evidence: Hosea describes Israel's past Exodus. Matthew's quotation and retelling are explicit but do not independently confirm the family’s travel. The timing of the quotation within Matthew is a real interpretive issue.
records.sourceStatus: Earlier reference to Israel explicit; later typological use explicit
refs: TheTorah: Hosea 11 and Israel as a child
Yale Bible Study: Matthew and new Exodus
Seong-Kwang Kevin Kim (2019), The Use of Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15

records.label: Rachel weeping for her children
records.kind: Exile lament later reapplied
records.original: רָחֵל מְבַכָּה (Rachel is weeping)
records.setting: Rachel personifies grief for Israelite exile; the very next lines promise that the children will return from enemy territory.
records.laterUse: Matthew quotes the lament when narrating Herod's killing of Bethlehem's boys.
records.relationship: A poetic lament in an exile-restoration context is given a new narrative referent.
records.evidence: The reuse is explicit and the original exile context can be verified. Matthew's particular massacre narrative is not independently established by this scriptural quotation.
records.sourceStatus: Different historical referents documented; event evidence limited
refs: TheTorah: Jewish origins of Christmas story

records.label: A ruler from Bethlehem
records.kind: Future royal oracle
records.original: בֵּית־לֶחֶם אֶפְרָתָה (Bethlehem Ephrathah)
records.setting: Micah looks toward a ruler emerging from David's ancestral setting amid political insecurity, with hopes of peace and protection for Israel.
records.laterUse: Matthew explicitly quotes Micah as identifying the Messiah's Bethlehem connection; Luke also places the birth in Bethlehem but supplies a different journey narrative and does not use the same fulfillment formula.
records.relationship: The earlier passage is a genuine future-oriented royal oracle, later understood christologically.
records.evidence: Micah contains a forward-looking Davidic royal oracle. The Bethlehem association may refer to Davidic origins as well as a locality; the two later nativity accounts do not supply independent contemporary corroboration of Jesus' precise birthplace.
records.sourceStatus: Earlier royal oracle clear; Bethlehem birth details unverified independently

records.label: The king riding a donkey
records.kind: Future royal oracle
records.original: עַל־חֲמוֹר וְעַל־עַיִר (on a donkey, and on a colt)
records.setting: Zion is told to welcome a humble, victorious king, contrasted with military power and associated with the end of war in the next verse.
records.laterUse: Mark and John describe one colt/donkey; Matthew names both a mother donkey and colt while citing Zechariah. What the pronoun 'them' refers to in Matthew 21:7 is also debated.
records.relationship: There are competing explanations: Matthew may have read Zechariah's poetic parallelism as two animals (Yale's account); Tucker Ferda (2020) argues Matthew combined Zechariah 9:9 with Genesis 49:10–11; Adam Kubiś (2018) defends a historically two-animal scene. Zechariah's Hebrew parallel phrases need not refer to two mounts.
records.evidence: Matthew's two-animal version is a textual fact. Its relationship to the one-animal accounts and the event itself is debated, so the Gospel quotation alone does not independently establish the exact incident.
records.sourceStatus: Textual reuse explicit; exact event details not independently established
refs: Tucker S. Ferda (2020), Journal of Theological Studies

records.label: The suffering servant
records.kind: Servant poem later identified with Jesus
records.original: עַבְדִּי (my servant; Isaiah 52:13)
records.setting: The servant poem belongs to Isaiah 40–55's exile-and-restoration setting. Isaiah 49:3 explicitly calls the servant Israel, but Isaiah 49:5 also describes a servant commissioned to restore Israel. This complicates a simple identification; views include collective Israel, an individual representative, or an idealized servant.
records.laterUse: New Testament texts apply servant phrases to Jesus' healings, suffering, death, and perceived redemptive role.
records.relationship: Later interpretation identifies the servant with Jesus; interpretations of the original figure include collective Israel and individual or idealized servants.
records.evidence: New Testament identification of the servant with Jesus is explicit. Even if Jesus' execution is accepted historically, it does not independently prove that the poem originally referred to him or that its theological portrayal of suffering was an advance prediction.
records.sourceStatus: Servant identity debated; New Testament application documented
refs: Hebrew Isaiah 49:5, servant commissioned to restore Israel

records.label: My God, why have you forsaken me?
records.kind: Lament psalm later reused
records.original: כָּאֲרִי (Masoretic 'like a lion') / כארו (Naḥal Ḥever variant): Hebrew Psalm 22:17, often 22:16 in English Bibles
records.setting: Psalm 22 is an anguished prayer of a suffering speaker who ultimately voices praise, not a prose forecast naming a future crucifixion.
records.laterUse: Jesus' cry and the distribution of garments are narrated with language that evokes Psalm 22; Christians also connect the debated hands-and-feet reading to crucifixion.
records.relationship: The evangelists echo an earlier lament, including its opening cry and imagery. The Masoretic text has 'like a lion'; a Naḥal Ḥever fragment supports a spelling with final waw; the Greek ὤρυξαν is 'they dug'. Translating the verbal tradition as 'pierced' is interpretive and disputed.
records.evidence: Hopkin (2005) argues that the ancient fragment supports the verbal reading; Strawn (2000) stresses the lion imagery and textual difficulties; NET translation notes challenge 'pierce' as a gloss. Competing textual readings do not by themselves show that Psalm 22 originally predicted Jesus' crucifixion.
records.sourceStatus: Ancient reading variation documented; prophetic status is interpretive
refs: Brent A. Strawn (2000), Journal of Biblical Literature

records.label: The voice in the wilderness
records.kind: Restoration oracle and punctuation
records.original: קֹול קֹורֵא בַּמִּדְבָּר (a voice calls: in the wilderness...)
records.setting: Second Isaiah (Isaiah 40–55) is commonly situated in the sixth-century BCE exilic context. Hebrew poetry pairs 'in the wilderness' with 'in the desert'; the voice calls for a processional road prepared for YHWH's return to the people.
records.laterUse: Gospel authors use the Greek textual tradition so that the voice belongs to John the Baptist in the wilderness.
records.relationship: The Septuagint does not reproduce the Hebrew 'in the desert' parallel phrase in the second line, enabling 'in the wilderness' to describe the crying voice. The Gospels apply that Greek reading to John the Baptist. The shift involves the Greek version's wording as well as punctuation.
records.evidence: Hebrew parallelism and Greek translation structure support distinct construals; the New Testament application is explicit. The earlier text does not name John the Baptist.
records.sourceStatus: Literary and translation shift documented
refs: David M. Freidenreich, TheTorah (2026): Hebrew and Greek compared

records.label: Babylon's predicted conquest of Egypt
records.kind: Historical prediction checked against external records
records.original: לָבוֹא נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּר ... לְהַכּוֹת אֶת־אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם (Nebuchadnezzar coming to strike Egypt)
records.setting: The oracle imagines a destructive Babylonian invasion and devastation of Egypt after Babylon's military rise.
records.laterUse: Later interpreters may regard partial raids as fulfillment or understand the oracle as revised in light of events.
records.relationship: A concrete military forecast, testable with Egyptian and Babylonian evidence and the book's editorial history.
records.evidence: Babylon fought Egypt and conducted raids; Egyptian independence continued until Persian conquest. Dan'el Kahn argues parts of the present prophetic text were revised with later Egyptian civil-war knowledge.
records.sourceStatus: Predicted full conquest not documented; partial attacks documented; textual layers debated

records.label: Egypt uninhabited for forty years
records.later: Egyptian historical record of the sixth century BCE
records.kind: Time-specified judgment oracle
records.original: אַרְבָּעִים שָׁנָה (forty years)
records.setting: The prophecy predicts devastation, dispersion, and lack of inhabitants for forty years, associated with Egyptian and Babylonian power.
records.laterUse: The forty-year desolation can be read as a literal timetable or as a rounded/rhetorical period. Ezekiel 29:17–21 offers Egypt as compensation for Nebuchadnezzar's inadequate reward from his campaign against Tyre; historical conquests require outside evidence.
records.relationship: Specific forecast compared to independent historical records, with attention to whether numbers are literal or rhetorical.
records.evidence: No independently verified Egyptian history supports forty years of the entire country being uninhabited. Babylonian attacks occurred, but the available record does not establish complete depopulation on the prophesied scale. Interpretive debate remains over the imagery and intended literalness.
records.sourceStatus: Literal fulfillment unsupported by known independent record
refs: Dan'el Kahn (2022), Egyptian and Babylonian evidence

records.label: Forty days until Nineveh's overthrow
records.kind: Conditional warning, not fixed timetable
records.original: עֹוד אַרְבָּעִים יֹום (yet forty days)
records.setting: The story has Jonah announce impending destruction; the city's response leads the narrator to say God does not bring the announced disaster.
records.laterUse: Sometimes claimed as failed prediction or defended as a conditional warning.
records.relationship: A teaching story about judgment and mercy, paired with Jeremiah's explicit principle that warnings may be conditional.
records.evidence: The narrative itself says the announced disaster did not occur. It gives a reason within the story; this does not independently establish that Jonah preached to historical Nineveh or that its repentance happened.
records.sourceStatus: Non-occurrence and conditional logic explicit within the narrative

records.label: He will be called a Nazarene
records.kind: Fulfillment formula with no identifiable antecedent
records.original: Ναζωραῖος κληθήσεται (Greek Matthew 2:23, 'he will be called a Nazarene'); no corresponding Hebrew prophecy text is known
records.setting: Matthew refers to what 'the prophets' said in the plural, but no extant verse in the Hebrew Bible makes this exact statement. Proposed connections include the Hebrew 'branch' (netser) in Isaiah 11:1, the Nazirite tradition, or a broader motif of social contempt; each has lexical or contextual obstacles.
records.laterUse: Matthew says Joseph's family settled in Nazareth so that the words spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled.
records.relationship: A fulfillment claim without a securely identifiable prior passage. An association with an older scriptural theme is plausible, but reconstructing an exact lost quotation or the author's motive exceeds the evidence.
records.evidence: Matthew 2:23 is verifiable. The lack of an extant matching oracle prevents word-for-word comparison or independent confirmation that 'Nazarene' was predicted; proposed Hebrew wordplays remain hypotheses.
records.sourceStatus: Fulfillment claim explicit; original quoted source unidentified

records.label: Great light in Galilee
records.kind: Restoration oracle applied to Jesus' Galilean ministry
records.original: הָעָם הַהֹלְכִים בַּחֹשֶׁךְ רָאוּ אוֹר גָּדוֹל ('people walking in darkness saw a great light')
records.setting: The Isaiah passage names the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali in northern Israel after devastation associated with imperial warfare in the eighth century BCE; its original horizon is hope after crisis. Its precise literary layering and royal expectation are debated.
records.laterUse: Matthew quotes the passage after Jesus relocates to Capernaum and begins his ministry in Galilee, identifying his activity with the light reaching the north.
records.relationship: The application is explicit; Matthew adapts the geographical and metaphorical imagery to Jesus. The earlier oracle does not name Jesus or specify a first-century Capernaum ministry.
records.evidence: The Hebrew text, its historical north-Israel setting, and the textual correspondence with Matthew are checkable. Matthew's report of the ministry cannot be treated as independent proof of supernatural fulfillment simply because Matthew supplies the citation.
records.sourceStatus: Earlier northern-restoration imagery and later application documented; supernatural forecast unverified
refs: Richard Beaton, Isaiah's Christ in Matthew's Gospel (2002), research program

records.label: He took our infirmities
records.kind: Healing formula quotation; lexical difference across Hebrew and Greek
records.original: חֳלָיֵנוּ הוּא נָשָׂא וּמַכְאֹבֵינוּ סְבָלָם ('our sicknesses he bore, our pains he carried')
records.setting: Isaiah's fourth servant poem depicts a sufferer bearing illness and pain, interpreted within the larger exile-restoration discourse. The ancient Greek version renders a related clause using 'sins', making the textual tradition crucial.
records.laterUse: Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4 after reporting Jesus' healings and exorcisms, drawing attention to physical sickness in the wording; this is a narrower use than later applications to Jesus' death.
records.relationship: A particular use of Isaiah 53 distinct from the broader servant-identity case already in this audit (isaiah-53). Matthew's phrasing is closer to the Hebrew's physical-illness sense than the old Greek version's 'sins'. Rikk Watts (2015) connects it to Matthew's wider theme of ending Israel's afflictions.
records.evidence: The verbal source and Hebrew–Septuagint difference are independently inspectable. Matthew's literary explanation for healings does not independently establish that the reported miracles occurred, nor prove an original forecast of Jesus.
records.sourceStatus: Explicit citation and identifiable translation choice; specific theological significance debated
refs: Rikk Watts (2015), Journal for the Study of the New Testament

records.label: The quiet servant bringing justice
records.kind: Servant-justice oracle applied to Jesus
records.original: הֵן עַבְדִּי ... מִשְׁפָּט לַגּוֹיִם יוֹצִיא ('Here is my servant ... he will bring justice to the nations')
records.setting: Isaiah's servant is characterized as chosen and Spirit-supported, bringing justice without destructive force; the servant's identity across Isaiah 40–55 is debated, and the text belongs to an exile/restoration horizon.
records.laterUse: Matthew quotes a lengthy adapted version to interpret Jesus' healing and instruction, including his restraint and the prospect of justice or hope among the nations.
records.relationship: Explicit later identification with Jesus. The Greek wording used in Matthew differs in places from both the standard Hebrew and the old Greek Isaiah text; it is an interpretive quotation rather than an exact unedited reproduction.
records.evidence: The passage's servant/justice language exists earlier, and Matthew's theological application is documented. Richard Beaton (2000) argues that the servant's justice is integral to Matthew's compassionate portrayal of Jesus; the original identity and fulfillment standard are debatable.
records.sourceStatus: Text-to-text use direct; earlier servant identity and fulfillment interpretation disputed
refs: Richard Beaton (2000), Matthew's use of Isaiah 42
Richard Beaton, Isaiah's Christ in Matthew's Gospel (2002)

records.label: I will open my mouth in parables
records.kind: Historical teaching psalm described as fulfilled
records.original: אֶפְתְּחָה בְמָשָׁל פִּי ('I will open my mouth with a parable')
records.setting: Psalm 78, associated by its superscription with Asaph, introduces a poetic instruction that retells Israel's past and teaches coming generations. In its own context it describes the psalmist's mode of teaching rather than a named future person's preaching.
records.laterUse: Matthew cites the line to explain Jesus' choice to teach in parables. Matthew's longer wording mentions what was hidden since the foundation of the world, whereas Hebrew Psalm 78:2 speaks about things 'from of old'.
records.relationship: A later literary application of ancient wisdom and teaching language, not an unambiguous predictive oracle. Some Greek manuscripts name Isaiah as the 'prophet' in Matthew 13:35; most do not. The source remains Psalm 78:2.
records.evidence: The older psalm and Matthew's citation are directly comparable; the choice of literary quotation does not independently prove historicity of every speech of Jesus. NET and NABRE textual notes document the rare Matthew 'Isaiah' variant.
records.sourceStatus: Earlier retrospective instruction and later reuse established; minor NT textual variant noted
refs: Yale Bible Study on Matthew's parables

records.label: Thirty silver pieces attributed to Jeremiah
records.kind: Composite attribution and redaction of a shepherd oracle
records.original: שְׁלֹשִׁים כָּסֶף ('thirty [pieces of] silver', Zechariah 11:12); Matthew says 'through Jeremiah'
records.setting: Zechariah 11 presents a symbolic shepherd drama about the rejection of a shepherd and the contemptuous thirty-silver payment. It mentions disposing of the money in the house of YHWH, but not the purchase of a potter's field.
records.laterUse: Matthew's Judas narrative specifies thirty silver pieces, money thrown into the temple, and the purchase of a potter's field; Matthew 27:9 calls the quotation Jeremiah although its closest wording is Zechariah 11:12–13.
records.relationship: The discrepancy is explicit. Some scholars posit composite imagery from Jeremiah 19 or 32; Maarten J. J. Menken (2002) argues Zechariah 11:13 is the main source and Matthew's redaction explains the altered wording and selected narrative details.
records.evidence: The source attribution in Matthew is demonstrably different from the best matching earlier text. A correction based solely on Matthew's own claim that Judas acted this way would be circular; the earlier source independently exists, but the thirty-coin event is not independently verified by that correspondence.
records.sourceStatus: Zechariah source and Jeremiah attribution verifiable; precise cause of misattribution debated

records.label: Good news, liberation, and the omitted day of vengeance
records.kind: Fulfillment declaration combining Hebrew Bible passages through Greek wording
records.original: רוּחַ אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה עָלָי (Spirit of the Lord YHWH is upon me); Luke draws on Greek Isaiah 61 and 58
records.setting: Isaiah 61 addresses the restoration community with news of liberation, comfort, and reversal; 61:2 includes both a favorable year and a day of divine vengeance. Isaiah 58:6 speaks of release from oppression in a critique of unjust fasting.
records.laterUse: Luke depicts Jesus reading an Isaianic scroll in Nazareth and declaring 'Today this scripture has been fulfilled'. Luke's Greek passage features sight for the blind from the Old Greek, adds a release line from Isaiah 58:6, and stops before the day-of-vengeance clause.
records.relationship: Explicit fulfillment claim with a composite quotation, selection and omission. Timothy Michael Law (2013) identifies the Septuagint sources; scholars debate whether omitting vengeance signals Luke's editorial theological emphasis.
records.evidence: The differences between Isaiah's Hebrew, Old Greek, and Luke's quotation are directly visible. The narrated synagogue encounter establishes Luke's literary depiction, not independently verified firsthand testimony about a historical speech.
records.sourceStatus: Quote and editorial changes directly checkable; historical speech uncorroborated
refs: Greek and Hebrew comparison (with Timothy Michael Law 2013)

records.label: Afterward becomes in the last days
records.kind: Future Spirit oracle reread as Pentecost fulfillment
records.original: וְהָיָה אַחֲרֵי־כֵן ('and it shall be afterward')
records.setting: Joel anticipates restoration and God's Spirit poured upon people of differing ages and genders after the communal crisis described in the book; the vision also includes cosmic signs and judgment.
records.laterUse: Acts' Peter says the Pentecost events are what Joel spoke about. Acts 2:17 introduces Joel's prophecy as occurring 'in the last days' rather than the Hebrew passage's simpler 'afterward'.
records.relationship: Explicit prophetic identification and interpretive temporal framing. The addition 'in the last days' matters for how the narrator places Pentecost inside eschatological history.
records.evidence: The textual wording and narrative use are independently checkable. Acts is a later report of the event being interpreted; it does not alone provide an independent verification of miraculous Spirit outpouring or the completion of cosmic signs.
records.sourceStatus: Original/Acts time-language difference confirmed; supernatural fulfillment a faith claim

records.label: Edom possessed or humankind seeking God?
records.kind: Greek translation changes the actors in a restoration oracle
records.original: לְמַעַן יִירְשׁוּ אֶת־שְׁאֵרִית אֱדוֹם (so they may possess the remnant of Edom)
records.setting: The closing oracle of Amos envisions restoration of David's fallen structure and renewed relationships with Edom and the nations. Its exact dating, possible editorial growth, and whether it envisages conquest or broader inclusion are discussed in scholarship.
records.laterUse: Acts presents James citing a Greek form in which 'the rest of humankind' seek the Lord, supporting the inclusion of Gentiles without requiring them to become Jews.
records.relationship: The Septuagint has 'seek' and 'humankind' in place of Hebrew 'possess' and 'Edom'. These are major grammatical and semantic changes, often explained through similar Hebrew letters and alternate vocalization; however, the phrase 'all the nations who are called by my name' is shared, so inclusion does not depend solely on the new Greek subjects.
records.evidence: Hebrew Amos, Old Greek, and Acts 15 can be compared. James D. Nogalski (2015) traces three stages of the text's interpretation. The Acts account itself is not independent proof the earlier author foresaw a specific first-century council.
records.sourceStatus: Substantial source-language difference documented; exact translation-history mechanism debated
refs: James D. Nogalski (2015), Three Faces of Hope
Septuagint/Hebrew details as secondary comparative source

records.label: Look on the one they pierced
records.kind: Piercing oracle and divergent Greek/Hebrew wording
records.original: וְהִבִּיטוּ אֵלַי אֵת אֲשֶׁר־דָּקָרוּ ('they will look toward me whom they pierced' in the Masoretic Text)
records.setting: In Zechariah 12, the house of David and inhabitants of Jerusalem are part of a future conflict, divine deliverance and communal mourning. The identity of the pierced figure and the relationship between first- and third-person phrasing are debated.
records.laterUse: John quotes the oracle immediately after describing a soldier piercing Jesus' side; Revelation 1:7 echoes it when describing Jesus' appearance.
records.relationship: The verb in John's quote is closer to Hebrew 'pierced' than the ancient Greek Zechariah's markedly different expression. John's Greek also frames the object in third person while the Masoretic text includes 'to me'. Whether John translated Hebrew directly or used an available Hebraizing Greek form is unproven.
records.evidence: The verbal parallels and variants are checkable. Christian and Jewish readings identify the subject differently. An independently accepted execution by crucifixion does not establish that the original Zechariah oracle specifically foretold John's narrative detail.
records.sourceStatus: Original and later wording documented; intended historical identity and textual route disputed
refs: Adam Kubiś on Zechariah in John (2012)

records.label: A new covenant for Israel and Judah
records.kind: New covenant promise applied to later Christian religious community
records.original: וְכָרַתִּי ... בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה ('I will make ... a new covenant')
records.setting: Jeremiah promises the houses of Israel and Judah a renewed covenant, in which divine teaching or Torah is internalized and sins are forgiven, as part of a restoration sequence after exile.
records.laterUse: Hebrews quotes Jeremiah at length to argue that a new priestly or covenantal order has become available through Jesus; Hebrews 8:13 says the earlier order is becoming old and approaching disappearance.
records.relationship: Explicit reuse and reinterpretation. Scholars disagree about how far Hebrews' language extends to replacing Judaism or Israel's covenant; Nicholas J. Moore (2024) argues the immediate argument centers on cultic aspects and warns against translating its Greek as a blanket denunciation of Judaism.
records.evidence: The shared wording is observable. The earlier text specifically names Israel and Judah; it does not name Jesus. Religious conclusions about superseding Judaism depend on later interpretation, and there is no independent historical observation that can confirm a divine covenant transfer.
records.sourceStatus: Quotation documented; theological and supersessionist readings disputed
refs: Nicholas J. Moore (2024), Supersessionism and the Cult Attitude of Stephen and Hebrews
Ted Goshorn (2016), Emory thesis on non-supersessionist covenant readings
